title: Estimation and Maximum Likelihood
intro: An estimator is a rule that turns data into a guess for a parameter. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter that makes the observed data most probable, and for large samples it is close to the best possible.

blocks.text: Data $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are modelled as i.i.d. from a distribution with unknown parameter $\theta$. An estimator $\hat\theta$ is any function of the data. Its quality is measured by its bias $E[\hat\theta] - \theta$ and its variance, combined in the mean squared error: $\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{bias}^2 + \mathrm{variance}$. A biased estimator can beat an unbiased one: dividing a sum of squares by $n + 1$ instead of $n - 1$ gives a smaller MSE for normal data.

blocks.caption: The likelihood is the joint density of the observed data, read as a function of the parameter.

blocks.text: Taking logs turns the product into a sum, and setting the derivative (the score) to zero usually gives the estimator. For a Bernoulli parameter it is the sample proportion; for an exponential rate, one over the sample mean; for a normal variance, the average squared deviation (dividing by $n$, so slightly biased). Maximum likelihood is invariant: the MLE of $g(\theta)$ is $g(\hat\theta)$.
Fisher information and the large-sample theory

The Fisher information $I(\theta) = -E[\ell''(\theta)]$ for one observation measures how sharply the likelihood peaks. Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal: $\hat\theta\approx N(\theta, 1/(nI(\theta)))$. The Cramér–Rao bound says no unbiased estimator has smaller variance than $1/(nI(\theta))$, so for large samples the MLE is as good as it gets. The approximation gives the standard confidence interval $\hat\theta\pm1.96/\sqrt{nI(\hat\theta)}$, which covers the true value in about 95% of repeated experiments. A confidence interval is a statement about the procedure, not about this particular interval.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(30)
# MLE of an exponential rate: lambda_hat = 1 / sample mean; Fisher information n / lambda^2
lam, n = 2.0, 50
data = rng.exponential(1 / lam, n)
lam_hat = 1 / data.mean()
se = lam_hat / np.sqrt(n)
print(f"lambda_hat = {lam_hat:.3f}, approximate standard error {se:.3f}, 95% CI ({lam_hat - 1.96*se:.3f}, {lam_hat + 1.96*se:.3f})")
# Repeat the experiment: how often does the 95% interval cover the true rate?
hats = 1 / rng.exponential(1 / lam, (20000, n)).mean(1)
cover = np.mean(abs(hats - lam) < 1.96 * hats / np.sqrt(n))
print(f"coverage over 20000 repeats: {cover:.3f}; bias of lambda_hat: {hats.mean() - lam:+.4f} (exact n/(n-1) factor: {lam * n / (n - 1) - lam:+.4f})")
# Method of moments vs MLE for a Uniform(0, theta): MLE is the sample maximum
theta = 10.0
u = rng.uniform(0, theta, (20000, 20))
mle, mom = u.max(1), 2 * u.mean(1)
print(f"Uniform(0,10), n = 20: MLE max mean {mle.mean():.3f}, MSE {np.mean((mle - theta)**2):.3f}; moments 2*mean MSE {np.mean((mom - theta)**2):.3f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: from 50 exponential observations with true rate 2, the MLE is 1.94 with standard error 0.27 and 95% interval (1.40, 2.48). Over 20 000 repetitions the interval covers the true rate 95.0% of the time, and the MLE is biased upwards by 0.040, matching the exact factor $n/(n-1)$. For Uniform(0, 10) with 20 observations, the MLE (the sample maximum) is biased low (mean 9.53) yet has mean squared error 0.43, against 1.65 for the unbiased method-of-moments estimator $2\bar x$.

blocks.title: Bernoulli MLE and its information
blocks.text: Find the MLE of $p$ from $k$ successes in $n$ Bernoulli trials, and the Fisher information per trial.
solution: $\ell(p) = k\ln p + (n - k)\ln(1 - p)$; setting $\ell' = 0$ gives $\hat p = k/n$.
$-\ell''$ for one trial has expectation $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{1-p} = \frac{1}{p(1-p)}$. So the standard error is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

blocks.title: Normal MLE
blocks.text: Find the MLEs of $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ for a normal sample.
solution: $\hat\mu = \bar x$ and $\hat\sigma^2 = \frac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$, which has expectation $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$.

blocks.title: Invariance
blocks.text: From exponential data with sample mean 4, what is the MLE of the median lifetime?
solution: By invariance, the MLE of the median is $4\ln2\approx2.77$.
